notes: Full administrative court judgment on final warning scheme; claim dismissed on all three challenged decisions.

enrichment.short_title: 14-year-old's judicial review of police refusal to administer final warning after aggravated vehicle taking

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Court Services Act 2000

key_facts: A 14-year-old claimant was one of five youths arrested after a stolen Rover Metro was pursued and damaged in Birkenhead in January 2003; two co-accused received reprimands but he was charged with aggravated vehicle taking after refusing to admit the offence in interview.

After charge, his solicitors indicated he might admit guilt and sought a final warning, but Merseyside Police declined to re-interview him and refused to administer a final warning; the CPS continued the prosecution.
The claimant sought judicial review of the police decisions and the CPS decision to pursue prosecution, contending breach of the final warning scheme and Home Office guidance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review hearing before Jackson J, with Rose LJ, following permission granted on the papers by Moses J.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; police lawfully declined re-interview and final warning; CPS lawfully continued prosecution; no costs order against the legally aided claimant.
enrichment.ratio: Section 65 of the Crime and Disorder Act 1998 requires an unequivocal admission to a constable before a final warning; police and CPS retain broad discretion where a young person denies guilt in interview and only later intimates admissions, and judicial review will rarely interfere with CPS prosecution decisions unless clearly contrary to settled policy.
legal_issues: Whether police could lawfully re-interview the claimant after charge under PACE Code C paragraph 16.5
Whether police were obliged or entitled to administer a final warning after solicitors indicated a possible admission
Whether the CPS acted irrationally in continuing prosecution after declining police recommendation of a final warning

notes: Interim injunction application in patent and passing off dispute over minocycline MR capsules.

enrichment.short_title: Wyeth interim injunction to restrain Alpharma launch of look-alike Minocin MR competitor
key_facts: Wyeth sought an interim injunction to prevent Alpharma launching Sebomin MR, a modified-release minocycline antibiotic for acne marketed as a substitute for Wyeth's Minocin MR under EP0 310814.
Alpharma's capsules and blister packs closely resembled Wyeth's distinctive orange and brown get-up, although outer packaging differed.
Alpharma had delayed launch several times after Wyeth raised patent and passing off concerns; the parties agreed the case could be ready for trial in about four months.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application for interim injunction before Laddie J in the Patents Court.
enrichment.outcome: Interim injunction granted preserving status quo pending trial; Alpharma restrained from launching Sebomin MR.
enrichment.ratio: Where both infringement and passing off are triable issues and validity cannot reliably be determined at the interlocutory stage without expert evidence, the court should apply American Cyanamid and grant relief to preserve the status quo rather than conduct a mini-trial on obviousness.
legal_issues: Whether Wyeth had an arguable case of patent infringement of controlled-release minocycline claims
Whether Alpharma's validity attack on Bechgaard prior art could be determined at the interlocutory stage
Whether Wyeth had protectable goodwill in capsule get-up and likelihood of confusion
Balance of convenience between price erosion and further launch delay

notes: Judicial review refusing technical lifer status; Article 6 held inapplicable to Secretary of State's administrative designation.

enrichment.short_title: Life-sentenced prisoner refused technical lifer status after missed paranoid schizophrenia diagnosis
key_facts: The claimant was convicted of manslaughter in 1997 and sentenced to life imprisonment with an eight-year tariff; at sentencing only one of three psychiatrists thought a hospital order possible and the statutory conditions for section 37 were not satisfied.
After transfer to hospital in 2000 and again in 2003, clinicians agreed he suffered paranoid schizophrenia; Dr Bullard acknowledged the primary diagnosis had been missed in 1997.
The Secretary of State refused technical lifer status, treating him as a discretionary life prisoner rather than as if sentenced to a hospital order with restrictions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review and Human Rights Act claim before Munby J, with interim injunction restraining return to prison pending judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; Article 6 challenge failed; Secretary of State lawfully applied technical lifer policy; injunction discharged.
enrichment.ratio: Designation as a technical lifer is an administrative post-sentence decision comparable to conditional release or clemency, not a sentencing exercise engaging Article 6; hindsight that medical evidence understated mental illness at trial does not show the sentencing court would or could have made a hospital order without two doctors agreeing mental illness warranted hospital detention.
legal_issues: Whether technical lifer designation is a sentencing exercise requiring a court under Article 6
Whether the Secretary of State misapplied his technical lifer policy where subsequent evidence suggested inaccurate 1997 psychiatric reports
Whether inadequate reasons or irrationality vitiated the refusal decision

notes: Court of Appeal on Quickfit conservatory design rights ownership; main appeal allowed on employment point but companies held beneficial owners via trust.

enrichment.short_title: Ultraframe appeal on ownership of Quickfit conservatory design rights created by sole shareholder designer
key_facts: Gerald Howard Davies designed the Quickfit conservatory roof system through successive companies he wholly owned and controlled; after bankruptcy and disqualification, disputes arose over ownership of design rights between Ultraframe, Northstar, Seaquest, and the Fieldings' Burnden Group.
Laddie J held at preliminary issues that Davies was employed by the companies and that design rights never belonged to Davies or his trustee, dismissing Ultraframe's London action.
Ultraframe appealed only the employment finding; respondents relied alternatively on commissioning and constructive trust.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from Laddie J's preliminary issues judgment, with a related cross-appeal on reserved costs.
enrichment.outcome: Main appeal allowed: Davies was not employed under a contract of service; design rights held on trust for the relevant companies; costs reservation order upheld; cross-appeal on costs dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A 100% shareholder-director who creates designs using company assets is not necessarily an employee for section 215(3) CDPA 1988 absent mutuality and control, nor are designs created pursuant to commission without prior contractual obligation; where a director creates designs for the company using its resources, he holds design rights on trust for the company and cannot rely on Duomatic assent to retain them beneficially where that would amount to an ultra vires distribution.
legal_issues: Whether Davies was an employee so that design rights vested in the Quickfit companies under section 215(3)
Whether designs were created pursuant to a commission under section 215(2)
Whether Davies held design rights on constructive trust for the companies
Whether Laddie J erred in reserving preliminary issue costs to the trial judge

notes: High Court permission to withdraw contact application in intractable private law dispute; full public judgment given.

enrichment.short_title: Father permitted to withdraw contact application after 12-year-old's sustained refusal
key_facts: Since 1998 the father had pursued contact with his son O through county court and High Court proceedings, including enforcement attempts, supervised contact, mediation, and psychiatric evidence.
Multiple judges found the father rigid and unable to accept responsibility for O's resistance; child psychiatrist Dr B advised direct contact would be counter-productive and harmful.

On the eve of a three-day final hearing the father applied to withdraw contact proceedings, accusing the mother, CAFCASS, and the courts of misconduct; the mother and CAFCASS Legal did not oppose withdrawal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under FPR 1991 rule 4.5(1) for permission to withdraw Children Act contact proceedings, following transfer from county court.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to withdraw granted; direct contact terminated for the foreseeable future with limited indirect contact; interim prohibited steps order continued pending judgment delivery.
enrichment.ratio: Termination of direct contact is a last resort where a non-resident parent's conduct, not parental alienation by the resident parent, has caused the child to resist contact; courts will permit withdrawal when continuing proceedings would harm the child and no realistic prospect exists of restoring contact without fundamental change by the applicant.
legal_issues: Whether the court should grant permission to withdraw contact proceedings
Whether the mother had alienated O from the father
Whether the father's conduct rather than the court system caused contact breakdown
Whether joint residence orders or continued litigation would promote O's welfare

notes: Criminal appeal on summing up structure in 10kg cocaine importation trial; convictions upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Cocaine importation appeals dismissed over structured summing-up and interview direction
key_facts: Millard and Middleton were convicted of being knowingly concerned in importing ten kilograms of cocaine after Dudley Edge brought the drugs from Spain and packages were recovered at Middleton's Loughton home and elsewhere in April 2000.
The Crown case relied heavily on telephone contact schedules and observations; both appellants denied involvement in cocaine importation, Middleton claiming a counterfeit clothing pickup.

The trial judge structured his summing up by defendant rather than summarising the Crown case first; Middleton also complained the judge failed to direct that Millard's police interview was inadmissible against him.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against conviction after trial at Isleworth Crown Court before HHJ McDowall and a jury.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals against conviction dismissed; summing up held fair and balanced; omission of specific interview direction did not render Middleton's conviction unsafe.
enrichment.ratio: A judge may structure a summing up around individual defendants where the Crown case is already encapsulated in schedules and admissions, provided burden and standard of proof directions are clear; failure to give a specific direction that one co-defendant's interview is inadmissible against another does not necessarily undermine safety where the overall direction on inadmissibility was given elsewhere.
legal_issues: Whether the summing up reversed the burden of proof by emphasising cross-examination over Crown case summary
Whether the judge adequately summarised the Crown case and defined issues
Whether Millard's police interview should have been directed as inadmissible against Middleton

confidence.notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment analysing summing up structure and specific Middleton interview point.

notes: Appeal from Pensions Ombudsman on AF80 discontinuance valuation; Ombudsman's maladministration findings and direction quashed.

enrichment.short_title: Legal & General appeal against Pensions Ombudsman over AF80 surrender value disclosure
key_facts: CCA Stationery Ltd's pension scheme used L&G's AF80 with-profits policy; in 1992 the trustees discontinued and chose cash on discontinuance, receiving about £3m against a nominal Total Cash Pool of about £3.7m.

The Pensions Ombudsman found maladministration because L&G did not disclose the full MVAF calculation process and because working papers for April 1992 MVAFs were lost; he directed appointment of an independent actuary.
L&G appealed, contending MVAF setting was not scheme administration, contractual rights were outside the Ombudsman's remit, and the direction exceeded court powers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court (Chancery) from a Pensions Ombudsman determination dated 9 December 2002, adjourned for balanced argument after Etherton J requested Ombudsman participation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; maladministration findings set aside; Direction to appoint independent actuary held ultra vires.
enrichment.ratio: Setting monthly value adjustment factors for L&G's Long Term Fund is not an act of administration of an individual AF80 pension scheme and therefore lies outside the Pensions Ombudsman's maladministration remit; the Ombudsman cannot make directions the court could not make, including delegating fact-finding to an independently appointed actuary.
legal_issues: Whether refusal to disclose MVAF methodology was maladministration of the pension scheme
Whether loss of internal MVAF working papers was maladministration
Whether calculation of cash on discontinuance was an act of scheme management
Whether the Ombudsman's direction to appoint an independent actuary was within his statutory powers

notes: Theft conviction quashed for lack of appropriation; remaining counts and leave application refused.

enrichment.short_title: Elderly victims' house proceeds theft conviction quashed for absence of appropriation
key_facts: Linda Briggs helped elderly Mr and Mrs Reid sell their Felixstowe home and arranged transfer of £49,950 of sale proceeds to complete purchase of Welwynd Lodge, which was registered in her and her father's names contrary to the Reids' expectations.
She was convicted of theft of the credit balance, forgery of tenancy agreements, dishonestly obtaining housing benefit, and obtaining a mortgage by deception.
The Reids had signed a letter of authority instructing the conveyancers to transfer £49,950 to Metcalfs for the purchase, but the prosecution alleged consent was procured by fraud.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against conviction on count 1 (theft), with renewed application for leave to appeal on remaining counts after partial grant by the Single Judge.
enrichment.outcome: Theft conviction on count 1 quashed; no substituted deception verdict under section 3 Criminal Appeal Act 1968; renewed application for leave to appeal on counts 3-7 refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where a defendant fraudulently induces the owner to instruct payment from the owner's account, the owner or the owner's agent effects the transfer and there is no appropriation by the defendant for theft purposes; such conduct is more appropriately charged under the Theft Act 1968 deception provisions.
legal_issues: Whether causing payment of sale proceeds by induced consent amounts to appropriation under section 3(1)
Whether a deception offence verdict should be substituted under section 3 Criminal Appeal Act 1968
Whether there was no case to answer on forgery, benefit fraud and mortgage deception counts

confidence.notes: Clear Court of Appeal analysis on appropriation with detailed treatment of remaining counts.

notes: CCRC referral on unused witness evidence; conviction on pool-cue ABH count upheld as safe.

enrichment.short_title: CCRC-referred appeal dismissed where defence chose not to call unused cue evidence
key_facts: Philip Hall was convicted at Guildford Crown Court in 1998 of affray and two assaults occasioning ABH after a pub fight involving pool cues; count 4 concerned a serious eye injury to Gary Reed.
The prosecution case on count 4 was that Hall, as the only person using a pool cue as a weapon, must have struck Reed; co-defendant Ayrton was acquitted on the equivalent count.

The Criminal Cases Review Commission referred the case because unused statements suggested Ayrton, not Hall, may have wielded a cue, but Hall's trial defence had been that no one used a cue on Reed and injury could have been caused by glass.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction on count 4 only, referred by the Criminal Cases Review Commission under section 23(1) Criminal Appeal Act 1968.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction held safe; unused evidence rightly not adduced at trial.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh or unused evidence will not render a conviction unsafe where competent trial counsel deliberately did not adduce it because it was inconsistent with the defence case actually run and would have created a cut-throat defence benefiting the prosecution.
legal_issues: Whether the court should admit unused witness statements under section 23(1) Criminal Appeal Act 1968
Whether failure to cross-examine Bowers on Ayrton carrying a cue or to call Simon Wood made the conviction unsafe
Whether the trial defence strategy precluded reliance on evidence implicating Ayrton as cue wielder

confidence.notes: Complete appellate judgment explaining why unused statements were incompatible with the defence run at trial.

notes: Winding-up petition and summary judgment in duty-suspended alcohol diversion fraud; very long judgment with clear dispositive findings.

enrichment.short_title: Customs winding-up of Arena over £1.8m excise debt and summary judgment against controller Schroeder

statutes_considered.title: Excise Duty Points (Duty Suspended Movements of Excise Goods) Regulations 2001

key_facts: HM Customs and Excise presented a winding-up petition against The Arena Corporation Ltd for £1,833,649.77 in excise duty and VAT after 19 consignments of duty-suspended alcohol were diverted from bonded warehouses using false accompanying administrative documents.
Peter Schroeder, Arena's beneficial owner, claimed Arena was engaged in legitimate trading with customers Celers and Euronet, with cash payments received in the UK by associate Paul Judd.

The judge found Schroeder's account incredible, with forged Italian customs stamps, inconsistent payment records, minimal warehouse contact, and no real prospect of success on Arena's VAT and Duties Tribunal appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Contested winding-up petition and provisional liquidator's summary judgment application heard together before Lawrence Collins J in the Companies Court.
enrichment.outcome: Winding-up order made against Arena; summary judgment for the provisional liquidator against Schroeder with £500,000 interim payment and post-judgment freezing order.
enrichment.ratio: Where duty-suspended alcohol is diverted using false AADs and a company controller's evidence is inherently incredible, neither a bona fide dispute on the excise debt nor a real prospect of defending a misfeasance claim will resist winding up or summary judgment.
legal_issues: Whether Arena's excise and VAT liability was disputed on genuine and substantial grounds
Whether Schroeder was complicit in diversion fraud through Arena
Whether summary judgment was appropriate on the provisional liquidator's claim against Schroeder
Application of DSMEG Regulations and Directive 92/12/EEC to deemed place of irregularity
